newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sends message to Croatia with IMF abstention.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sends message to Croatia with IMF abstention.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it abstained voting on a new International Monetary Fund loan to Croatia to send a strong message of displeasure with Zagreb's failure to turn over indicted war criminals to the Hague tribunal for prosecution.

"To express our displeasure with the Croatian government, to send a shot across their bow that we do want them and expect them to implement the Dayton Accords, we abstained on the vote earlier this week at the IMF," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

The IMF on Thursday said it approved a three-year, $486 million loan for Croatia to support the nation's economic reform plan. The plan, which covers the period 1997 to 1999, aims to cement the progress that has been made in stabilizing the economy and help the country rebuild itself after the war.

Explaining the U.S. position on the loan, Burns said: "There are a number of indicted war criminals who live in Croatia who have not been turned over to the war crimes tribunal by the Croatian government ... You need to go in and arrest them and turn them over to the tribunal. The Croatian government has failed to do that."

U.S. officials said privately that while they have general concerns about Croatia's failure to cooperate with the war crimes tribunal in the Hague, abstaining on the $486 million IMF loan related specifically to the case of one individual, Zlatko Aleksovski.
Aleksovski has been in Croatian custody since June but authorities have refused to transfer him to the Hague, arguing that he is ill, one official said.
Legally, this is a valid argument only if the prisoner physically cannot be moved and "we are supporting tribunal efforts to get some type of confirmation," the official said.
She added that doctors representating the tribunal were expected in Zagreb soon to examine Aleksovski.

The United States has been looking at ways to encourage greater cooperation with the war crimes tribunal. Abstaining on the Croatia loan "was obviously a symbolic gesture. We did not vote against the loan," Burns acknowledged.
"It was symbolic but sometimes symbolism, coupled with stronger measures down the road, if compliance is not met, get the attention of governments like the government of Zagreb," he said.
